stem: Why do reported national disability prevalence statistics vary significantly across different countries?

options.text: National surveys are carried out mainly in countries that have ratified the CRPD.
options.rationale: Censuses and national surveys are fielded in countries regardless of whether they have ratified the CRPD, so ratification cannot explain the differences.

options.text: Countries differ in how they define disability and ask survey questions.
options.rationale: Differences in how disability is defined in law and how survey questions are worded account for large differences in reported national rates.

options.text: Most countries estimate prevalence from hospital admission records rather than population surveys.
options.rationale: National prevalence figures usually come from population censuses and surveys, not from hospital admission records.

options.text: Countries count disability benefit recipients as equal to the number of people with disabilities.
options.rationale: Benefit receipt depends on eligibility rules and programme coverage, so it does not equal the number of people with disabilities.

explanation: There is no standardized way of measuring disability. Countries define disability differently in law, word survey questions differently, and set different thresholds for counting a person as disabled, so reported national rates are not directly comparable. Many people also have more than one disability, which makes them hard to place in a single category.
